summary: Describes the procedure and IANA guidelines for defining new DHCP options and message types. It is a Best Current Practice document.

eli5.summary: This explains how someone can get a new setting added to the official list of DHCP settings, and what they need to prepare.

questions: how to define a new dhcp option
how to get a new dhcp option number
which dhcp option codes are private use
subtitle: How a new DHCP option or message type gets a number: write a draft, get IESG review, and receive a code when the RFC is published.

tldr.problem: DHCP option numbers 1-127 were almost used up, many assigned numbers were never followed by a specification, and the older rules did not require individual review or say that options must not be used before publication.
tldr.mechanism: A new option or message type is written up as an Internet Draft with its code marked TBD, reviewed by the DHC Working Group or IETF and the IESG, and given a code by IANA only when it is published as an RFC.
tldr.outcome: Codes are assigned by IETF consensus from a single authority, and the procedure also covers new message types, which RFC 2131 had no mechanism for. It replaces RFC 2489.

today: RFC 2939 is a Best Current Practice (BCP 43) and the unit metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. It obsoleted RFC 2489.

sections.title: Why a Procedure Is Needed
sections.content:
DHCP passes configuration information to hosts in tagged data items stored in the options field of a DHCP message. The items are themselves called options. DHCP messages are identified by the DHCP Message Type option (option code 51), and each message type is a data value carried in that option.

New options and message types can be defined after the DHCP specification was published. RFC 2939 describes how. The procedure is meant to guarantee three things: option and message type numbers are coordinated by a single authority, new items are reviewed for technical correctness and appropriateness, and their documentation is complete and published. IANA acts as that central authority and this document guides it in assigning codes.
sections.eli5: There has to be one keeper of the list, so two people never pick the same number and every entry is written down properly.

sections.title: Problems With the Old Process for Options
sections.content:
This document modifies and clarifies the procedure for defining options in RFC 2131. The main change is when an option number is assigned: not until the specification is about to be published as an RFC.

The RFC gives the reasons. Since the publication of RFC 2132, the public option number space (1-127) had almost been exhausted. Many assigned numbers were never followed by an Internet Draft submitted to the DHC Working Group, and IANA had no specific guidance from the working group on assigning numbers.

RFC 2132's procedure also did not clearly say that each new option is reviewed for technical correctness, appropriateness and complete documentation. It did not require submission to the IESG or make the option's author responsible for bringing it to the IESG's attention. It also did not make clear that new options must not go into products, other specifications or other use until the specification is published as an RFC.
sections.eli5: People kept grabbing numbers and never finishing the paperwork, so the numbers were running out. The new rules say no number until the paperwork is done.

sections.title: Public and Site-Specific Option Codes
sections.content:
In the future, new option codes are assigned by IETF consensus. Options are documented in RFCs approved by the IESG, and the code is assigned when the RFC is published. The IESG typically seeks input from appropriate sources, such as a relevant Working Group. Related options may be combined into one specification and reviewed as a set. Before a code is assigned, it is not appropriate to build the option into products, cite it in other documents or otherwise use it.

The option number space (1-254) is split in two. The site-specific codes (128-254) are "Private Use" and need no DHC WG review. They MUST NOT be defined for use by any publicly distributed DHCP server, client or relay agent implementation, because they are reserved for private use within a site or organization. The public codes (0-127, 255) are "Specification Required", so new options must be reviewed before IANA assigns a number.
sections.eli5: Half the numbers are public and need approval. The other half are like a private notebook for one school or company, and products sold to everyone must never use them.

sections.title: The Five-Step Procedure
sections.content:
The same steps apply to new options and new message types, and RFC 2939 makes this explicit for message types, for which RFC 2131 specified no mechanism. The author takes these steps.

  1. The author devises the new option or message type.
  2. The author documents it as an Internet Draft, leaving the code as "To Be Determined" (TBD). The RFC says the Internet Draft form is a matter of expediency, since the specification will end up as one during review anyway.
  3. The author submits the draft for IESG review, preferably through the DHC Working Group, though going directly to the IESG is allowed. Publishing a draft does not by itself bring it to the IESG's attention, so the author must explicitly request action.
  4. The IESG reviews the specification, and the DHC WG (if it exists) or the IETF reviews it too. If accepted, it is published as an RFC, which may be standards-track or non-standards-track.
  5. At the time of publication as an RFC, IANA assigns the option code or message type code.

As with options, it is not appropriate to use a new message type in products or other specifications before its code is assigned.
sections.eli5: Write your idea down with a blank where the number goes, ask the leaders to look at it, and when it is officially published you get your number filled in.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
Information that creates or updates an option code or message type code assignment needs to be authenticated. Every newly defined option or message type needs an analysis of its security issues, and the description must be as accurate as possible.

A specification may simply reference the Security Considerations section of the DHCP specification. The RFC quotes the NetWare/IP option specification (RFC 2142) as an example: DHCP currently provides no authentication or security mechanisms, and potential exposures are discussed in section 7 of the DHCP protocol specification.
sections.eli5: Every new setting must say what could go wrong, and only the right people may change the official list.

sections.title: Instructions to IANA
sections.content:
RFC 2132 and RFC 2489 had given IANA guidance on assigning option numbers for new options or message types. RFC 2939 updates and replaces those instructions.

IANA is asked to assign option codes or message type codes only for items approved for publication as RFCs, that is, documents approved through "IETF consensus" as defined in RFC 2434.
sections.eli5: The keeper of the list is told: only hand out a number once the leaders have approved the written description.

sections.title: Changes From RFC 2489
sections.content:
RFC 2939 obsoletes RFC 2489, "Procedure for Defining New DHCP Options". It extends that procedure to cover the definition of new DHCP message types as well as options.

It also strengthens the language reserving the site-specific option codes, to stress that those codes must not be encoded in publicly distributed DHCP implementations.
sections.eli5: The old rulebook only covered settings. The new one also covers message kinds, and it says louder that the private numbers stay private.

items.label: Public
items.desc: Specification Required: reviewed before IANA assigns a number.

items.label: Site-specific
items.desc: Private Use: no DHC WG review, and MUST NOT be defined in publicly distributed implementations.
